## Place mimicry-js generators directly as field values, use Faker inside arrow functions

_critical · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Put `oneOf`, `sequence`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `unique` and `withPrev` directly as a field value
or inside a static nested object. Inside an arrow function, use the Faker equivalent instead, for
example `faker.helpers.arrayElement([...])` for `oneOf`.

**Why.** mimicry-js resolves generators only where it walks the `fields` object. An arrow function's body is
opaque to it, so a generator returned from one ends up in the built object as a descriptor. The
test then compares against an object, not a string, and the failure message points nowhere near
the builder.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
fields: {
  profile: () => ({ theme: oneOf("light", "dark") }),
}
```

**Correct:**

```ts
fields: {
  theme: oneOf("light", "dark"),
  profile: () => ({ theme: faker.helpers.arrayElement(["light", "dark"]) }),
}
```

## Make every test able to fail when the behaviour it names breaks

_critical · any_

**Rule.** End every test with an assertion that would fail if the behaviour in its name broke. Before you
trust a new test, check that it can fail: break the condition it checks, or assert the opposite,
and see it go red.

**Why.** A test that only renders and clicks, or asserts something that is always true, stays green while
the feature is broken, so the suite reports coverage that does not exist.

## Wait for a condition the user would see, never for a fixed time

_critical · any_

**Rule.** When the result of an action arrives later, wait for the condition itself: a query that retries
until the element appears, or a retrying assertion on the value or call you expect. Give a long
operation a longer timeout on that wait instead of a sleep before it.

**Why.** A fixed sleep is too short on a slow CI machine and too long everywhere else, so the suite is both
flaky and slow, and its failures name the assertion after the sleep instead of what never happened.

## Set every value the test asserts on explicitly when you build test data

_high · any_

**Rule.** Build test data from a builder or factory, and pass an explicit override for every field the test
asserts on or branches on. Leave random values only in fields the test never looks at. Use named
variants (traits) for whole states such as "admin" or "inactive" instead of repeating the same
overrides in many tests.

**Why.** An assertion against a randomly generated value passes or fails depending on the seed, and a
reader cannot tell from the test which value matters. An explicit override documents the input the
test depends on and makes the failure reproducible.

## Wrap function-typed fields in fixed() so the builder does not call them

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** For a field whose value is itself a function (`onClick`, `onSubmit`, a formatter), wrap the
function in `fixed(fn)`. Leave a bare arrow function only where you want a fresh value on each build.

**Why.** mimicry-js calls any function it finds as a field value, so a bare callback is replaced by its return
value and the built object has `undefined` where a handler should be.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const buttonPropsBuilder = build<ButtonProps>({ fields: { label: "Save", onClick: () => {} } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const buttonPropsBuilder = build<ButtonProps>({ fields: { label: "Save", onClick: fixed(() => {}) } });
```

## Build with .one() and .many() and pass overrides or traits for asserted values

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Call `.one({ overrides })` for a single object and `.many(count, { overrides })` for a list.
Define recurring states as `traits` in the builder and apply them with `.one({ traits: "admin" })`.
The builder methods are `.one()` and `.many()`, not `.build()` or `.buildMany()`.

**Why.** Hand-written objects drift from the type, and `Array.from()` loops skip traits and overrides.
Calling methods that do not exist on a mimicry-js builder is the drift this note was written to
stop.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const user = userBuilder.build();
const users = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => userBuilder.build());
await expect(canvas.getByText(user.name)).toBeVisible();
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const user = userBuilder.one({ overrides: { name: "Ada Lovelace" } });
const admins = userBuilder.many(3, { traits: "admin" });
await expect(canvas.getByText("Ada Lovelace")).toBeVisible();
```

## Write TypeScript builders with mimicry-js and Faker

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Write every TypeScript builder with `build<T>()` from `mimicry-js`, with `@faker-js/faker` for
realistic values. Name it `camelCase(TypeName) + "Builder"` in a `kebab-case.builder.ts` file, and
migrate test-data-bot or Fishery builders when you touch them.

**Why.** Two builder libraries in one codebase mean two APIs for overrides and traits, and tests copied from
one style break when pasted next to the other.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const makeUser = (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User => ({ id: "1", name: "Ada", ...overrides });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const userBuilder = build<User>({
  fields: { id: () => faker.string.uuid(), name: () => faker.person.fullName() },
});
```

## Keep the unit under test real, and change the test rather than the code

_high · any_

**Rule.** Mock only what the unit under test depends on, never the unit itself. When a new test fails, fix
the test; if the failure shows a real defect in the code, report it instead of editing the code or
weakening the assertion to make the test pass.

**Why.** A mocked or quietly patched unit makes the test check itself: it passes while the shipped code is
still broken, and the bug it found disappears from view.

## Find elements the way a user or a screen reader does

_high · any_

**Rule.** Locate elements by their role and accessible name first, then by their label, then by visible
text. Reach for a test id only when the element has no accessible identity at all, and fix the
component when that is because its semantics are wrong.

**Why.** A test that finds a button by its role and name keeps passing through any refactor that keeps the
button usable, and fails when a user could no longer find it. A test that finds it by class name or
test id breaks on harmless markup changes and stays green when the accessible name disappears.

**Exceptions.** A test id is fine for an element with correct semantics that still has nothing stable to query by, such
as dynamic text and no role. It beats a CSS class, because it makes the link between test and code explicit.

## Make every test pass alone and in any order

_high · any_

**Rule.** Write each test so it passes when run alone and in any order. Configure and reset mocks before each
test, and share repeated setup through a small helper function, never through a mutable variable
that tests write to.

**Why.** A test that leans on an earlier one passes in the full run and fails when filtered or reordered,
which shows up as a flaky suite whose failures point at the wrong test.

## Mock only what a test cannot run or could only run with great difficulty

_high · any_

**Rule.** Mock something only when the test could not be written without the mock or would be very awkward with
the real thing. In UI tests that means the network, animations, and services with a real cost or effect
such as payments and e-mail. In E2E tests it means almost nothing.

**Why.** Every mock cuts the link between the tested code and what it replaced, so the suite stays green when
that link breaks in production.

## Reproduce a bug with a failing test before fixing it

_high · any_

**Rule.** When a bug earns a test, write the test that reproduces it before touching the code, and see it fail.
Decide whether it earns one the way you prioritise any other work, by what the breakage costs users.

**Why.** A regression test written after the fix may never have failed, so it can pass without covering the bug,
and the bug comes back with the test still green.

**Exceptions.** A bug that costs users little, in a place that is expensive to test, can get a fix with no test.

## Spend most testing effort on integration tests

_high · any_

**Rule.** Give integration tests the largest share of testing effort, keep E2E tests to the happy paths of
critical flows, use unit tests for pure functions and complex logic, and leave typos and wrong types
to static analysis. Choose the layer by the problem: a calculator edge case is a unit test, a form
submit with validation is an integration test, logging in through the whole app is an E2E test.

**Why.** A suite of isolated unit tests stays green while the pieces fail to work together, and a suite of E2E
tests is too slow and costly to reach the edge cases. Static analysis does not replace either, because
it cannot see a wrong business rule.

**Exceptions.** This holds for one codebase, a frontend or a monolith. It says nothing about a microservice architecture.

## Test only what the end user or the developer using the code can touch

_high · any_

**Rule.** Write tests against what the code's two users have: the rendered output an end user sees and clicks,
and the props and providers a developer passes in. When a refactor that keeps the behaviour forces a
test to change, rewrite that test so it stops depending on the implementation.

**Why.** A test that knows state, handler names or component structure fails on a harmless refactor and passes
when the feature is broken, and the code ends up serving a third user that nobody needs.

## Reset builder counters and random state between tests that depend on them

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When a test depends on a generated sequence value or on seeded random output, reset the builder's
counters and seed before each such test. Tests that only use explicit overrides need no reset.

**Why.** Counters and random state live as long as the builder module. A test that expects `id: 1` passes
alone and fails when another test ran first, which shows up as an order-dependent, flaky suite.

## Build structured test data with a builder, not inline object literals

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Take typed test data with three or more fields, nested objects or lists from a builder. Look for an
existing builder first and create one only when none exists; never hand-roll a factory inside a test
or story file. Primitive values and objects with fewer than three fields may stay inline.

**Why.** Hand-written literals copied across tests drift from the type and from each other: adding a required
field breaks every copy, and each test fills the fields it does not care about differently.

## Fill nested typed objects from their own builder

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Give each nested type its own builder and use it as `field: () => otherBuilder.one()`. Override a single
nested key through the parent's `overrides`, which deep-merge, instead of rebuilding the nested object.

**Why.** A nested object written inline in the parent duplicates the child builder's defaults, and the two
drift until the same type looks different depending on which builder made it.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const orderBuilder = build<Order>({
  fields: { customer: { id: "c1", name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.com" } },
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const orderBuilder = build<Order>({ fields: { customer: () => customerBuilder.one() } });
orderBuilder.one({ overrides: { customer: { name: "Ada Lovelace" } } });
```

## Build lists with .many(count), not Array.from or map

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Build a list of test objects with `builder.many(count, options)`. Pass overrides or traits through its
options instead of mapping over `Array.from` or a spread array.

**Why.** A hand-rolled loop skips the builder's list handling, so overrides and traits have to be repeated per
item and `unique()` values can collide across the list.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const users = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => userBuilder.one({ traits: "admin" }));
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const users = userBuilder.many(3, { traits: "admin" });
```

## Compute fields that derive from other fields in postBuild

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** When a field is computed from other fields of the same object (a total from line items, a full name
from first and last), compute it in the builder's `postBuild`, not in a field generator and not in
each test.

**Why.** A generated derived field ignores overrides of the fields it derives from, so an object built with
custom line items still carries a random total and the test asserts on an impossible object.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
fields: { items: () => itemBuilder.many(2), total: () => faker.number.int() }
```

**Correct:**

```ts
fields: { items: () => itemBuilder.many(2), total: 0 },
postBuild: (order) => ({ ...order, total: order.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0) }),
```

## Call builder.reset() in beforeEach when a test depends on sequence values

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** In a suite whose assertions depend on `sequence()` or `unique()` values, call `.reset()` on the
builder in `beforeEach`. Call `seed(value)` once when the test depends on the output of `oneOf`,
`int`, `float` or `bool`.

**Why.** Counters keep counting across tests in the same module, so `id: 1` is only true for whichever test
runs first.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
test("first order gets id 1", () => {
  expect(orderBuilder.one().id).toBe(1);
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  orderBuilder.reset();
});

test("first order gets id 1", () => {
  expect(orderBuilder.one().id).toBe(1);
});
```

## Use unique() for values that must differ across built objects

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** When every built object needs a distinct value from a fixed set (emails, slugs, keys in a list), use
`unique([...])` instead of `oneOf(...)`. Give it at least as many values as the test builds, and reset
the builder between tests that rely on the order.

**Why.** `oneOf()` picks at random, so a `.many()` call can return two objects with the same key, and the test
fails only on the runs where the duplicate happens.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const tagBuilder = build<Tag>({ fields: { slug: oneOf("news", "blog", "docs") } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const tagBuilder = build<Tag>({ fields: { slug: unique(["news", "blog", "docs"]) } });
```

## Assert what the user sees or can do, never internal state or markup

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Assert on what a user or assistive technology perceives: visible text, values, enabled or disabled
state, focus, ARIA attributes, and the calls a callback received. Leave internal state, class names
that carry no meaning for the user, and markup snapshots out of assertions.

**Why.** Tests that read internals break on every refactor that changes nothing for the user, and still pass
when the user-facing behaviour is broken, so the suite stops being trusted.

## Keep test setup inline until repetition hides what differs between tests

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Write a test's data and setup inline first. Extract a helper once repetition hides what differs between
tests; it takes overrides and returns what the test needs, with no branch per case, so a reader sees the
difference between two similar tests at once.

**Why.** A shared helper with an `if` for every case makes the reader step through it to learn what one test does,
and copied setups bury the one line that differs.

## Derive the expected value from the test's own input, not a repeated literal

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the expected value follows from the test's input, compute it from that input: the row count
from the list the test rendered, a field's value from the value the test prefilled. Write a literal
only for a value the test introduces in the assertion itself.

**Why.** A hard-coded copy of the input goes stale the moment the input changes, so the test fails for a
reason unrelated to the code, or keeps passing against the wrong number.

## Keep snapshots small and inline, for output whose exact text matters

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Snapshot only small output whose exact text matters, such as error messages, logs or transformed code,
and keep the snapshot inline in the test. Replace a large snapshot with explicit assertions.

**Why.** A 600-line snapshot states no intent, so when it fails everyone overwrites it and moves on, and a real
regression goes in with the update.

## Query by the text users read, not by translation keys

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Query and assert on text as a user reads it in the default locale, never on the translation key behind it.

**Why.** A test that looks for `auth.username` still passes after the label changes from "Username" to "Email",
which is exactly the change a test should report.

## Use semantic HTML instead of adding ARIA so that a query works

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Use the semantic element and give inputs a `type`, so the implicit role is correct. Add `role` or
`aria-*` only for what HTML cannot express, and never just to make a test's query find an element.

**Why.** A `role="button"` on a `div` makes the query pass while the element still has no keyboard behaviour, so
the test reports an accessible control that users do not have. On a `button` the same attribute is noise.

## Choose the next test by what would hurt most if it broke

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Pick the next test by asking what in the untested part of the app would hurt most if it broke. Narrow
that to one or a few units of code, name who uses them, write the instructions you would give a manual
tester, and turn those instructions into the automated test.

**Why.** Tests chosen by walking through branches, loops and lifecycles cover code nobody would miss while the
checkout flow stays untested, so effort goes up and confidence does not.

## Judge a suite by the use cases it covers, not by a coverage percentage

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Use a coverage report only to find code without tests, and judge a suite by which use cases it covers.
Set no percentage target for an application, and do not measure coverage on E2E tests.

**Why.** A percentage target gets met with tests of the cheapest lines, so a suite can report 100% while an
unhandled use case ships broken.

**Exceptions.** A small open source library used in many places can justify aiming for 100%.

## Write the test first when the requirements are clear

_low · any_

**Rule.** Write the test first when the requirements are clear: pure functions, bug fixes, UIs with a well-defined
design. In exploratory coding, add the tests once the direction has settled.

**Why.** Tests written first during exploration get rewritten with every change of direction, and tests postponed
on clear requirements give up the fastest feedback available.
